[03:04] Sarah QA: Yeah, really well. I like everyone here. It's been a really good atmosphere lately, which is nice.
[03:10] Demo Manager: Good. And it does feel that way, doesn't it? It's good. Um, is there anything that's been difficult?
[03:18] Sarah QA: No. No, not with the team, no. I mean, you know, there was, there was a bit of a thing with one of the families last week, but it's related to the thing I want to talk to you about later.
[03:35] Demo Manager: Okay, well, we'll, we'll come to it. How are you feeling in yourself, well-being-wise?
[03:42] Sarah QA: Yeah, I'm good. I've actually been feeling more confident lately, like I know what I'm doing now. 18 months ago, I was quite anxious about a lot of things, but, but now I feel much more settled.
[03:56] Demo Manager: Yeah, it's really good to hear. It, it shows. I've, I've noticed your practice has become much more assured. Sandra mentioned you in the incident— after the incident last month with MR B. She said the way you handled that was really calm and professional.
[04:18] Sarah QA: Oh, that was just— I mean, anyone would have done the same.
[04:21] Demo Manager: Yeah, but they wouldn't though, Tracy. You, you stayed very calm. You knew exactly who to call and in what order, and you kept him comfortable throughout. That's not nothing. That deserves to be on record. That shows you understand the policy. You were able to follow the procedure. It's really good.
[04:44] Sarah QA: Thank you, it means a lot.
[04:46] Demo Manager: Right, is there anything on the training front coming up?
[04:51] Sarah QA: Yeah, I've got safeguarding refresher in September I'm already booked on, and I've been thinking about whether I do the senior care worker pathway. I've talked to my partner about it and they're supportive.
[05:06] Demo Manager: So that's brilliant. I'd love to put your name forward for that. You're exactly the kind of person we'd want to access that learning and development. Shall I, shall I get you, uh, shall I get you some more information?
[05:20] Sarah QA: Yeah, go on then. I think I'm ready. Brilliant.
[05:27] Demo Manager: Right, uh, I think we're ready for the, for the thing now, aren't we?
[05:32] Sarah QA: Well, yeah. Okay. So, um, I don't even know where to start with this. Um, I'm kind of worried I've done something wrong, but I'm also worried that something's been happening. So I need you to hear both things.
[05:53] Demo Manager: Okay, I'm, I'm listening. Take your time.
[05:57] Sarah QA: Right. There's a resident, MRS N. She's been here about 8 months. Lovely lady. She's got quite significant dementia, but she has good days, she has bad days. My son Son of Mrs N comes in a few times a week. Obviously, it's nice, it's good that he comes in and he visits, but yeah, well, there's something's not been sitting right with me for a while.
[06:28] Demo Manager: Okay, what, what kind of thing's not sitting right with you?
[06:34] Sarah QA: Well, little things at first. Son of Mrs N always asks to take her handbag away when he visits. He says he wants to make sure she doesn't lose anything, but MRS N gets very distressed when her handbag goes. It's, you know, it's her thing. She keeps bits and pieces in there that matter to her, and he kind of overrides it. He just takes it.
[07:03] Demo Manager: Right, okay, go on, tell me more.
[07:05] Sarah QA: And then about 3 weeks ago, Son of Mrs N came in and he had some paperwork. I couldn't see what it was, but he was asking MRS N to sign things, and she was asking him what she was signing, and he was saying it was just something for the bank, nothing to worry about. Um, And, you know, I walked past and something, you know, something just didn't feel right. It didn't look right.
[07:35] Demo Manager: Okay, what did you do when you saw that?
[07:39] Sarah QA: Wow, that's, you know, this is where I think I've done something wrong. I, I didn't say anything at the time, but I started, I started, I started keeping an eye out. And then, and this is the bit I'm worried about, I sort of asked MRS N on a couple of visits what she knew about her finances, like whether she had savings, that kind of thing. She got confused, but she said something about Son of Mrs N taking care of everything and that she used to have more money in her account. And I know I know I shouldn't have asked those things directly. I know that's not my role.
[08:24] Demo Manager: Okay, what else?
[08:26] Sarah QA: I— oh, you know, I'm a bit embarrassed about this. I had a chance when Son of Mrs N had taken her out for a short walk and her room was unlocked. I went in and I looked in the drawer of her bedside table. She had some letters in there, and I could see the top of What looked like a bank statement. I didn't read it fully. I just glanced. I know that was wrong. I know I shouldn't have done it.
[08:56] Demo Manager: Okay. Anything else?
[09:01] Sarah QA: Well, I told Deborah last week because it was going round and round and round, and I knew I needed to talk to somebody. I know I should have come straight to you, but I panicked a bit.
[09:15] Demo Manager: Okay, thank you for telling me all of this. Can I ask you what made you come to me today rather than sooner?
[09:22] Sarah QA: Because I realized I'd made it worse by doing what I did. I was just going to leave it and hope nothing happened, but then Son of Mrs N came in again yesterday and the same thing happened with the paperwork, and I thought if I don't say something now and something happens to her, I won't be able to live with myself.
[09:43] Demo Manager: Okay, well, I'm glad you told me. So I need to say a few things now, and I want you to hear all of them. So firstly, your instinct about MRS N, the things you've described— the handbag, the signing of paperwork under pressure, the comment about money— those are things that warrant a safeguarding referral. You were right to be concerned. That concern is legitimate. And I'm taking it seriously today.
[10:16] Sarah QA: Okay.
[10:17] Demo Manager: So secondly, the way you went about it, asking MRS N directly about her finances and going into her room when she wasn't there, looking at her personal correspondence, telling Deborah before you told me— those— none of those things were the right approach. I know they came from a good place. I know you weren't trying to cause harm, but they could cause harm. To MRS N, because she's been asked leading questions by someone in a position of authority over her care, any future safeguarding process, because evidence gathered and the way you gathered it could complicate things. And also to Deborah, who knows something she shouldn't know yet, and We'll need to manage that.
[11:12] Sarah QA: Yeah, I know. I'm sorry.
[11:16] Demo Manager: So I'm not saying this to make you feel bad. I'm saying it because you need to understand why the process matters. You know, it's not a policy thing. It's just it protects everyone, and it's important, including MRS N. Does that make sense?
[11:36] Sarah QA: Yeah, I think I knew all of that and I still did it because I was scared nothing would happen if I did it the right way.
[11:43] Demo Manager: Well, that's an honest answer and it tells me something. It tells me you don't trust the process. We'll need to work on that. But right now, I'm gonna start a safeguarding referral this afternoon. I'll need you to write down everything you observed, everything you did, and everything MRS N said as accurately and completely as possible, including the things that you did that you shouldn't have.
[12:12] Sarah QA: Even the drawer thing?
[12:15] Demo Manager: Especially the drawer thing. The referral needs to be honest, and we'll need to speak to, to Deborah today as well before the end of the shift.
[12:25] Sarah QA: Is Deborah gonna get in trouble?
[12:27] Demo Manager: Deborah hasn't done anything wrong. She was told something by a colleague We just need to make sure she understands the confidentiality position going forward.
[12:37] Sarah QA: Okay, what about me? Am I in trouble?
[12:42] Demo Manager: I'm not gonna pretend that there aren't things that need to be addressed here, Tracy, but I also want you to know that coming in here today and telling me all of this, including the difficult parts, is what good practice looks like. You could have said nothing. But you didn't. That's important. That matters.
[13:10] Sarah QA: I couldn't have said. I couldn't have said nothing. Not after yesterday.
[13:15] Demo Manager: I know, right? Let's make sure we've covered everything else before we finish, and then we'll go straight into the written account.
[13:24] Sarah QA: Okay. Um, there's one more thing. It's probably not relevant, but Son of Mrs N. When he visits, he sometimes goes through her drawers himself looking for things. The care staff have never really questioned it. I think it's just become normal.
[13:42] Demo Manager: That's relevant. Thank you. We need to write that down too.

analyses.summary:
Tracy, a care worker, and the home manager met for a scheduled one-to-one supervision session. They reviewed Tracy’s recent training and care-planning activities and then discussed a new concern regarding potential financial abuse of a resident.

- Tracy completed the mental health awareness module two weeks ago and found the section on recognising depression in older adults far more detailed and useful than expected.  
- Tracy updated the personal care section of Mr Salter’s care plan, flagged his change in mobility with Deborah, and reported that he seems much more settled since Deborah adjusted his moving and handling plan.  
- Tracy said her workload remains manageable but noted that Mrs Fairweather was unusually unsettled this week due to her son’s increased visits disrupting her routine, and she will record this pattern formally in the care plan.  
- The home manager praised Tracy’s calm and professional handling of last month’s incident with Mr Batt—citing Sandra’s feedback on Tracy’s prompt calls and comfort measures—and agreed it will be formally recorded.  
- Tracy has booked her safeguarding refresher training for September and expressed interest in the senior care worker pathway, and the home manager agreed to send her more information.  
- Tracy raised serious concerns that Mrs Novak’s son Brian repeatedly takes her handbag against her wishes, pressures her to sign paperwork of unknown content, and that Tracy later glanced at what appeared to be Mrs Novak’s bank statement, suggesting possible financial abuse.

The home manager will review and update Mrs Fairweather’s care plan with Tracy this week and send Tracy details on the senior care worker pathway by next Friday. They also agreed to make an immediate safeguarding referral about Mrs Novak’s finances and ensure all observations are documented and escalated through the adult protection team.

analyses.summary:
This transcript does not contain information about a UK adult social care supervision session, nor does it identify participants or their roles. The provided audio appears to be a brief test of headphones in an airport environment, not a professional meeting.

- The first speaker noted they were using Bose headphones in an airport, with planes clanking, as part of an audio test.
- The second speaker confirmed they were also wearing headphones to observe the outcome of this test.
- Both individuals expressed curiosity about the results of their headphone test in the noisy setting.

No outcomes or next steps related to adult social care supervision were discussed or agreed upon in this transcript. The content solely focused on an audio equipment test, without any professional context or actions.

Demo Manager and Demo User met for a supervision session to discuss Demo User's recent performance, well-being, and attendance, as well as celebrate his achievements. The session aimed to understand the context behind recent absences and explore support mechanisms.

- Demo User highlighted the success of his reminiscence sessions, noting positive impacts on residents like Mr P and Mrs OB, whose family and key worker (Sandra) have observed significant improvements in their engagement and mood.
- Demo User celebrated the successful sign-off of his NVQ unit on person-centred care, with Karen providing positive feedback on his practical application and helping him overcome challenges with the written reflection.
- Demo User expressed feeling a "vibe" or tension with another care worker, which Demo Manager acknowledged as a concern for his well-being and offered to monitor, encouraging Demo User to speak up if it escalates.
- Demo Manager addressed Demo User's three recent absences, which Demo User attributed to a genuine stomach bug, emotional exhaustion from a difficult week and extra shifts, and generally "not in a good place" due to feeling low on and off for a couple of months.
- Demo User shared that his father's health issues have been a significant worry and draining, leading to frequent weekend visits home and contributing to his overall stress.

Demo Manager will provide Demo User with details for the employee assistance program and strongly encouraged him to speak with his GP regarding his low mood. Demo Manager also committed to reviewing the rota this week to explore reducing Demo User's weekend shifts to alleviate pressure related to his father's health.

standards_entries.name: Staffing – overarching requirements
standards_entries.description: The service provider must ensure that at all times a sufficient number of suitably qualified, trained, skilled, competent and experienced staff are deployed. Must consider the statement of purpose, individual needs, personal outcomes and all other regulatory requirements. The staffing determination must be demonstrable and measurable.
standards_entries.keywords: ["staffing levels", "skill mix", "qualified staff", "competence", "deployment", "staffing determination", "care needs", "personal outcomes", "temporary staff", "agency staff", "nursing staff", "staff cover", "staffing policy"]
standards_entries.source: The Regulated Services (Service Providers and Responsible Individuals) (Wales) Regulations 2017 (as amended)

standards_entries.name: Fitness of staff
standards_entries.description: Service providers must not employ or allow anyone to work at the service unless they are fit to do so: suitable character, required qualifications/skills/experience, health, and satisfactory DBS checks. Care workers and managers must be registered with Social Care Wales. DBS checks must be renewed at least every 3 years.
standards_entries.keywords: ["fitness of staff", "DBS", "Disclosure and Barring Service", "Social Care Wales", "SCW registration", "character check", "qualifications", "skills", "experience", "references", "employment checks", "health assessment", "recruitment vetting"]
standards_entries.source: The Regulated Services (Service Providers and Responsible Individuals) (Wales) Regulations 2017 (as amended)

standards_entries.name: Supporting and developing staff
standards_entries.description: Service providers must have a staff support and development policy. All staff must receive: role-appropriate induction (AWIF within defined timescale), regular supervision (at least quarterly), annual appraisal, core training, and specialist training as appropriate. Staff must be supported to maintain professional registration with Social Care Wales.
standards_entries.keywords: ["induction", "AWIF", "All Wales Induction Framework", "supervision", "quarterly supervision", "appraisal", "annual appraisal", "training", "core training", "specialist training", "CPD", "professional development", "Social Care Wales registration", "staff development policy", "training needs analysis", "delegation"]
standards_entries.source: The Regulated Services (Service Providers and Responsible Individuals) (Wales) Regulations 2017 (as amended)

standards_entries.name: Compliance with employer's code of practice
standards_entries.description: The service provider must adhere to Social Care Wales's code of practice on the standards of conduct and practice expected of persons employing or seeking to employ social care workers (the Employer's Code of Practice).
standards_entries.keywords: ["employer's code of practice", "Social Care Wales", "SCW", "conduct standards", "employment standards", "code of practice", "workforce standards"]
standards_entries.source: The Regulated Services (Service Providers and Responsible Individuals) (Wales) Regulations 2017 (as amended)

standards_entries.name: Information for staff
standards_entries.description: All staff and volunteers must be provided with information about the service and how it is provided. Must include codes of professional practice, policies, confidentiality, safeguarding arrangements, lone working, and disciplinary procedures. Regular staff meetings (minimum 6 per year) must take place and be recorded.
standards_entries.keywords: ["staff information", "code of practice", "policies and procedures", "induction", "confidentiality", "data protection", "safeguarding awareness", "lone working", "staff meetings", "job description", "accountability"]
standards_entries.source: The Regulated Services (Service Providers and Responsible Individuals) (Wales) Regulations 2017 (as amended)

standards_entries.name: Disciplinary procedures
standards_entries.description: Service providers must have and operate a disciplinary procedure. Must include provision for suspension, and failure to report abuse is grounds for disciplinary action. Where an employee leaves before completion of disciplinary proceedings, providers must consider referral to DBS, Social Care Wales or police.
standards_entries.keywords: ["disciplinary procedure", "suspension", "misconduct", "reporting abuse", "DBS referral", "Social Care Wales referral", "police referral", "performance", "conduct", "grievance", "employment law"]
standards_entries.source: The Regulated Services (Service Providers and Responsible Individuals) (Wales) Regulations 2017 (as amended)

standards_entries.name: Records
standards_entries.description: Service providers must keep and maintain all records specified in Schedule 2 of the Regulations. Records must be accurate, up to date and kept securely. Adults' records retained for 3 years; children's for 15 years. Individuals must be able to access their own records. Electronic records must be password protected.
standards_entries.keywords: ["records management", "record keeping", "accuracy", "secure storage", "retention", "data protection", "GDPR", "individual access", "electronic records", "Schedule 2", "personal records", "staff records", "confidentiality"]
standards_entries.source: The Regulated Services (Service Providers and Responsible Individuals) (Wales) Regulations 2017 (as amended)

standards_entries.name: Complaints policy and procedure
standards_entries.description: Service providers must have an accessible complaints policy and effective arrangements for identifying, investigating and responding to complaints. Must include advocacy information (Llais/Citizen Voice Body), timescales, and written responses to complainants. Complaints must be analysed to identify areas for improvement.
standards_entries.keywords: ["complaints", "complaints policy", "complaints procedure", "investigation", "response timescales", "Llais", "Citizen Voice Body", "advocacy", "complainant rights", "complaints analysis", "trends", "service improvement", "Public Services Ombudsman", "whistleblowing"]
standards_entries.source: The Regulated Services (Service Providers and Responsible Individuals) (Wales) Regulations 2017 (as amended)

standards_entries.name: Whistleblowing
standards_entries.description: Service providers must have a whistleblowing policy and effective arrangements to enable staff to raise concerns about matters affecting individual health, safety or well-being. Concerns must be investigated, appropriate action taken, and a record kept. Staff must not suffer victimisation for raising concerns.
standards_entries.keywords: ["whistleblowing", "raising concerns", "staff concerns", "whistleblowing policy", "confidentiality", "investigation", "no victimisation", "safeguarding concerns", "duty of candour", "speak up", "transparency"]
standards_entries.source: The Regulated Services (Service Providers and Responsible Individuals) (Wales) Regulations 2017 (as amended)

standards_entries.name: Quality of care review
standards_entries.description: The responsible individual must establish and maintain a system for monitoring, reviewing and improving quality of care — at least every 6 months. The review must analyse engagement outcomes, incidents, safeguarding, whistleblowing, complaints and records audits. A report with assessment and recommendations must be prepared for the service provider.

standards_entries.description: People are supported to pursue meaningful activities, maintain relationships and fulfil personal goals and aspirations. standards_entries.description: The service provider must not agree to provide care unless the service is suitable to meet the individual's care and support needs and personal outcomes. standards_entries.keywords: ["mental health", "dementia", "behaviour", "wellbeing", "cognitive impairment", "anxiety", "depression", "positive attitudes", "reasonable adjustments"]
standards_entries.sub_outcomes: [{"ref": "9.1a", "desc": "Describe the main forms of mental ill health and their prevalence"}, {"ref": "9.2a", "desc": "Describe the key aspects of dementia including how it may affect the individual"}, {"ref": "9.3a", "desc": "Describe what is meant by learning disability and how it may affect an individual"}, {"ref": "9.4a", "desc": "Describe how the way an individual communicates may be affected by mental health, dementia or learning disability"}]

standards_entries.name: Safeguarding adults
standards_entries.description: The care worker understands adult safeguarding, recognises signs of abuse and neglect, and knows how to report concerns.
standards_entries.keywords: ["safeguarding", "abuse", "neglect", "reporting", "whistleblowing", "protection", "harm", "exploitation", "concerns", "restrictive practices"]
standards_entries.sub_outcomes: [{"ref": "10.1a", "desc": "Define the term 'safeguarding'"}, {"ref": "10.2a", "desc": "Describe the types of abuse and neglect and the signs and symptoms associated with them"}, {"ref": "10.3a", "desc": "Describe what to do if abuse of an adult is suspected"}, {"ref": "10.4a", "desc": "Describe the importance of ensuring individuals are treated with dignity and respect"}]
standards_entries.source: Care Certificate Standards 2025 - Skills for Care

standards_entries.name: Safeguarding children
standards_entries.description: The care worker is aware of child safeguarding responsibilities even when primarily working with adults.
standards_entries.keywords: ["safeguarding children", "child protection", "young carers", "children", "abuse", "neglect"]
standards_entries.sub_outcomes: [{"ref": "11.1a", "desc": "Describe the main duties and responsibilities in relation to safeguarding children"}, {"ref": "11.2a", "desc": "Identify signs of abuse and what to do if abuse is suspected"}]
standards_entries.source: Care Certificate Standards 2025 - Skills for Care

standards_entries.name: Basic life support
standards_entries.description: The care worker knows how to provide basic life support, including CPR, and can respond to emergency situations.
standards_entries.keywords: ["first aid", "CPR", "resuscitation", "basic life support", "emergency", "AED", "choking"]
standards_entries.sub_outcomes: [{"ref": "12.1a", "desc": "Describe when it would be appropriate to administer basic life support"}, {"ref": "12.2a", "desc": "Demonstrate the ability to perform CPR using appropriate equipment"}, {"ref": "12.3a", "desc": "Describe how to reduce the risk of infection when administering first aid"}]

standards_entries.name: Health and safety
standards_entries.description: The care worker understands health and safety legislation, risk assessment, moving and handling, medication, fire safety, security and personal wellbeing.
standards_entries.keywords: ["health and safety", "risk assessment", "COSHH", "moving and handling", "manual handling", "PPE", "lone working", "fire safety", "medication", "security"]
standards_entries.sub_outcomes: [{"ref": "13.1a", "desc": "Identify the health and safety legislation relevant to their role"}, {"ref": "13.2a", "desc": "Describe what is meant by a risk assessment and why they are carried out"}, {"ref": "13.3a", "desc": "Describe how to reduce the risk of accidents in the work setting"}, {"ref": "13.4a", "desc": "Describe what to do if an accident or incident occurs"}, {"ref": "13.5a", "desc": "Describe how to use PPE correctly to reduce risk of infection"}]
standards_entries.source: Care Certificate Standards 2025 - Skills for Care

standards_entries.name: Handling information
standards_entries.description: The care worker understands data protection, GDPR, confidentiality obligations, and maintains accurate, secure records.

standards_entries.sub_outcomes: [{"ref": "14.1a", "desc": "Identify the legislation and agreed ways of working in relation to recording, storing and sharing information"}, {"ref": "14.2a", "desc": "Describe how to maintain confidentiality in day-to-day communication"}, {"ref": "14.3a", "desc": "Describe the potential consequences of a breach of confidentiality"}]

standards_entries.description: The care worker understands and applies infection prevention and control measures, including hand hygiene, PPE, and standard precautions.

standards_entries.sub_outcomes: [{"ref": "15.1a", "desc": "Describe the routes by which infection can enter the body"}, {"ref": "15.2a", "desc": "Demonstrate how to carry out hand washing technique"}, {"ref": "15.3a", "desc": "Describe the correct procedures for using and disposing of PPE"}, {"ref": "15.4a", "desc": "Describe how to reduce the risk of spreading infection"}]

standards_entries.name: Awareness of learning disability and autism
standards_entries.description: It is a legal requirement that all staff working in CQC-regulated services undertake training on how to interact appropriately with people with a learning disability and autistic people, at a level appropriate to their role.

standards_entries.source: Care Certificate Standards 2025 - Skills for Care

standards_entries.description: Worker is able to: embed a rights-based approach in their practice with adults.

standards_entries.sub_outcomes: [{"ref": "1.11a", "desc": "Understands the impact of own attitude and behaviour on individuals and carers"}]

standards_entries.name: Agreement between service user and agency
standards_entries.description: Each service user has a written individual service agreement before care commences. The agreement must cover the services to be provided, fees, notice periods, and the complaints procedure. Service users must be supported to understand and consent to the agreement.

standards_entries.name: Recording and reporting
standards_entries.description: All activities undertaken in relation to the service user's care plan are recorded and relevant information communicated to appropriate people. Records must be accurate, up-to-date, and securely maintained. Significant incidents, changes in condition, and near misses must be reported promptly.
standards_entries.keywords: ["recording", "reporting", "care records", "documentation", "accurate records", "incident reporting", "near misses", "significant events", "communication", "information sharing", "data protection", "GDPR", "confidentiality"]

standards_entries.name: Contributing to service user reviews
standards_entries.description: The agency contributes to the review of the service user's care plan. Reviews must happen at agreed intervals or when needs change. The agency must involve the service user, carers and other professionals, and update care plans to reflect changing needs.
standards_entries.keywords: ["care plan review", "review process", "changing needs", "multidisciplinary", "involvement", "regular review", "care planning", "outcomes", "personal outcomes", "risk review"]

standards_entries.name: The appropriate use of control and restraint
standards_entries.description: Control or restraint may only be used to prevent risk of harm and must be proportionate. Must only be carried out by trained staff. Service providers must have a policy and must record any incident within 24 hours. Reviews must inform the quality of care review.
standards_entries.keywords: ["restraint", "control", "restrictive practice", "proportionate", "risk of harm", "trained staff", "positive behaviour support", "mental capacity", "deprivation of liberty safeguards", "DOLS", "recording incidents"]
standards_entries.source: The Regulated Services (Service Providers and Responsible Individuals) (Wales) Regulations 2017 (as amended)

standards_entries.name: Deprivation of liberty
standards_entries.description: Individuals must not be deprived of their liberty for care purposes without lawful authority. Service providers and staff must act in accordance with the Mental Capacity Act 2005 and Deprivation of Liberty Safeguards. Staff must receive training at appropriate intervals.
standards_entries.keywords: ["deprivation of liberty", "lawful authority", "Mental Capacity Act", "MCA 2005", "Deprivation of Liberty Safeguards", "DoLS", "best interests", "mental capacity", "consent", "authorisation", "liberty protection safeguards"]
standards_entries.source: The Regulated Services (Service Providers and Responsible Individuals) (Wales) Regulations 2017 (as amended)

standards_entries.name: Quality assurance and improvement is led well
standards_entries.description: Robust quality assurance systems are in place and actively used; improvements are evidence-based and clearly driven by outcomes for people; complaints, incidents and near-misses are analysed to drive learning; governance arrangements are transparent and effective. The service can demonstrate continuous improvement.
standards_entries.keywords: ["quality assurance", "governance", "audit", "monitoring", "continuous improvement", "complaints analysis", "incident analysis", "learning culture", "self-evaluation", "quality framework", "key performance indicators", "improvement planning"]
standards_entries.source: Care Inspectorate Scotland — Quality Framework for Care Homes for Adults and Older People (applicable across registered adult social care services)

standards_entries.name: Leaders collaborate to support people
standards_entries.description: Leadership works effectively with external agencies, commissioners, health professionals, social work, families and other partners to support people's individual outcomes. Partnership and integration arrangements are well-managed.
standards_entries.keywords: ["partnership", "multi-agency", "collaboration", "external agencies", "commissioners", "integrated care", "social work", "health professionals", "community links", "referral pathways"]
standards_entries.source: Care Inspectorate Scotland — Quality Framework for Care Homes for Adults and Older People (applicable across registered adult social care services)

standards_entries.name: Staff are led well
standards_entries.description: Staff receive regular, meaningful supervision and annual appraisal; communication is open and transparent; staff wellbeing is actively supported; leadership is visible, accessible and responsive. Staff feel valued, supported and confident to raise concerns.
standards_entries.keywords: ["supervision", "appraisal", "staff wellbeing", "open communication", "visible leadership", "team meetings", "whistleblowing", "speaking up", "staff support", "team culture", "staff engagement", "recognition"]
standards_entries.source: Care Inspectorate Scotland — Quality Framework for Care Homes for Adults and Older People (applicable across registered adult social care services)

standards_entries.name: Staff have been recruited well
standards_entries.description: Safer recruitment practices are followed; PVG (Protection of Vulnerable Groups) Scheme checks are in place for all relevant staff; thorough references are obtained; SSSC registration requirements are met before staff begin working; fitness to practise is assessed and maintained.
standards_entries.keywords: ["safer recruitment", "PVG", "Protection of Vulnerable Groups", "SSSC registration", "references", "induction", "fitness to practise", "employment checks", "pre-employment screening", "Disclosure Scotland"]
standards_entries.source: Care Inspectorate Scotland — Quality Framework for Care Homes for Adults and Older People (applicable across registered adult social care services)

standards_entries.name: Staff have the right knowledge, competence and development to care for and support people
standards_entries.description: Staff complete the National Induction Framework (NIF) and meet SSSC registration requirements including mandatory qualifications. Ongoing CPD is actively supported; training needs are systematically identified and met; staff can demonstrate competence and reflect on practice. Specialist training is provided as needed.
standards_entries.keywords: ["NIF", "National Induction Framework", "SSSC registration", "SVQ", "qualifications", "CPD", "continuing professional development", "competency", "training", "mandatory training", "specialist training", "reflection", "learning", "supervision"]
standards_entries.source: Care Inspectorate Scotland — Quality Framework for Care Homes for Adults and Older People (applicable across registered adult social care services)

standards_entries.name: Staffing arrangements are right and staff work well together
standards_entries.description: Staffing levels and skill mix are appropriate and safe at all times; staff work cohesively as a team; effective handovers ensure continuity of care; deployment decisions are driven by people's needs; temporary/agency staff are appropriately inducted and supervised.
standards_entries.keywords: ["staffing levels", "skill mix", "teamwork", "continuity of care", "handover", "shift patterns", "safe staffing", "deployment", "agency staff", "bank staff", "lone working", "team cohesion"]
standards_entries.source: Care Inspectorate Scotland — Quality Framework for Care Homes for Adults and Older People (applicable across registered adult social care services)

standards_entries.name: People experience high quality facilities
standards_entries.description: The physical environment is safe, well-maintained, clean and suited to the needs of the people who use the service. Equipment is appropriate, well-maintained and available. Health and safety requirements are met; fire safety, COSHH and risk assessments are in place.
standards_entries.keywords: ["facilities", "environment", "cleanliness", "maintenance", "equipment", "health and safety", "fire safety", "COSHH", "risk assessment", "premises", "accessibility"]
standards_entries.source: Care Inspectorate Scotland — Quality Framework for Care Homes for Adults and Older People (applicable across registered adult social care services)

standards_entries.name: The setting promotes people's independence
standards_entries.description: The environment is designed and managed to actively promote independence; assistive technology is used where appropriate; people can move freely and safely around the spaces available to them; the layout supports dignity and privacy.
standards_entries.keywords: ["independence", "assistive technology", "accessibility", "mobility", "layout", "privacy", "dignity", "enabling environment", "technology enabled care"]
standards_entries.source: Care Inspectorate Scotland — Quality Framework for Care Homes for Adults and Older People (applicable across registered adult social care services)

standards_entries.name: People can be connected to and involved in the wider community
standards_entries.description: The service actively supports people to maintain community connections, access local amenities and sustain relationships outside the service. Social isolation is proactively addressed; people are supported to be active citizens in their local community.
standards_entries.keywords: ["community connections", "social isolation", "community involvement", "outings", "volunteers", "family contact", "citizenship", "community activities"]
standards_entries.source: Care Inspectorate Scotland — Quality Framework for Care Homes for Adults and Older People (applicable across registered adult social care services)

standards_entries.name: Assessment and personal planning reflects people's outcomes and wishes
standards_entries.description: Individual assessments are thorough, person-centred and co-produced; personal plans are detailed, current and clearly reflect each person's outcomes, needs, wishes and choices; plans are reviewed regularly and when needs change; the person is central to all planning decisions.
standards_entries.keywords: ["personal plan", "care planning", "assessment", "personal outcomes", "co-production", "person-centred", "individual needs", "wishes", "review", "risk assessment", "positive risk", "informed decisions"]
standards_entries.key_questions: ["How well is our care and support planned?"]
standards_entries.source: Care Inspectorate Scotland — Quality Framework for Care Homes for Adults and Older People (applicable across registered adult social care services)

standards_entries.name: Carers, friends and family members are encouraged to be involved
standards_entries.description: Carers, family members and people important to the individual are actively included in assessment, care planning and reviews; their expertise about the person is valued; their own support needs as carers are recognised and addressed.
standards_entries.keywords: ["carers", "family involvement", "carer support", "carer assessment", "partnership", "relatives", "significant others", "inclusive planning", "carer rights"]
standards_entries.key_questions: ["How well is our care and support planned?"]
standards_entries.source: Care Inspectorate Scotland — Quality Framework for Care Homes for Adults and Older People (applicable across registered adult social care services)

standards_entries.name: Overall capacity for improvement
standards_entries.description: A global judgement based on evidence and evaluations from all other key questions. Assesses whether the organisation has the leadership, culture, resources and systems to sustain and improve quality over time. Takes account of contextual factors such as staffing changes, restructuring plans or significant funding changes.
standards_entries.keywords: ["capacity for improvement", "sustainability", "leadership capability", "change management", "resources", "culture of improvement", "self-evaluation", "track record", "forward planning", "resilience", "organisational health"]
standards_entries.key_questions: ["What is our overall capacity for improvement?"]
standards_entries.source: Care Inspectorate Scotland — Quality Framework for Care Homes for Adults and Older People (applicable across registered adult social care services)

standards_entries.name: Protect and promote the rights and interests of individuals and carers
standards_entries.description: Social service workers must work with kindness, compassion and respect; treat each individual as unique; respect and promote people's rights, views, wishes and choices; promote control and informed decision-making; use preferred communication methods; maintain dignity and privacy; and promote diversity and respect all identities, values and cultures.
standards_entries.keywords: ["rights", "interests", "compassion", "respect", "kindness", "dignity", "privacy", "choices", "individuality", "diversity", "identities", "values", "cultures", "preferred communication", "informed decisions"]
standards_entries.sub_outcomes: [{"ref": "1.1", "desc": "Work with kindness, compassion and respect and treat each individual as unique"}, {"ref": "1.2", "desc": "Respect and promote the rights and, where appropriate, the views, wishes and choices of individuals and carers"}, {"ref": "1.3", "desc": "Promote the rights of individuals to have control over their lives and make informed choices about their care or support"}, {"ref": "1.4", "desc": "Work with individuals and carers to communicate using their preferred method and language"}, {"ref": "1.5", "desc": "Respect and maintain the dignity and privacy of individuals"}, {"ref": "1.6", "desc": "Promote diversity and respect all identities, values and cultures"}]
standards_entries.source: Scottish Social Services Council — Code of Practice for Social Service Workers (2024)

standards_entries.name: Policies and procedures
standards_entries.description: There are comprehensive, up-to-date policies and procedures in place that direct the quality of care and services. All policies must be reviewed at least every three years, and staff must have access to and be familiar with relevant policies including safeguarding, medicines, and complaints.
standards_entries.keywords: ["policies and procedures", "policy review", "safeguarding policy", "medicines policy", "complaints policy", "health and safety policy", "lone working policy", "staff access", "knowledge of policies", "review cycle"]
standards_entries.source: RQIA — Domiciliary Care Agencies Minimum Standards (DHSSPS, August 2021)

standards_entries.name: Build and maintain the trust and confidence of individuals and carers
standards_entries.description: Social service workers must be truthful, open, honest and trustworthy; communicate respectfully and accurately; maintain confidentiality; be reliable and dependable; declare conflicts of interest; follow policies on gifts and money; and maintain professional boundaries that respect dignity, wellbeing and safety.
standards_entries.keywords: ["trust", "honesty", "openness", "transparency", "confidentiality", "reliability", "professional boundaries", "conflicts of interest", "dependability", "communication", "gifts policy"]
standards_entries.sub_outcomes: [{"ref": "2.1", "desc": "Be truthful, open, honest and trustworthy"}, {"ref": "2.2", "desc": "Communicate in a respectful, open, accurate and straightforward way"}, {"ref": "2.3", "desc": "Respect confidential information and clearly explain policies about confidentiality to individuals and carers"}, {"ref": "2.4", "desc": "Be reliable and dependable"}, {"ref": "2.5", "desc": "Honour work commitments, agreements and arrangements and explain why when not possible"}, {"ref": "2.6", "desc": "Declare issues that might create conflicts of interest and ensure they do not influence judgement or practice"}, {"ref": "2.7", "desc": "Follow policies and procedures about exchanging gifts and money with individuals and carers"}, {"ref": "2.8", "desc": "Form open, positive relationships and maintain professional boundaries with individuals, colleagues or carers"}]
standards_entries.source: Scottish Social Services Council — Code of Practice for Social Service Workers (2024)

standards_entries.name: Information for service users
standards_entries.description: Prospective service users are provided with information about the services provided by the agency before care commences. Information must be clear, accessible and in appropriate formats. Service users must understand their rights, the complaints procedure and how to access RQIA.
standards_entries.keywords: ["information provision", "accessible information", "prospective service users", "service guide", "rights", "complaints procedure", "RQIA contact", "formats", "language needs", "statement of purpose"]
standards_entries.source: RQIA — Domiciliary Care Agencies Minimum Standards (DHSSPS, August 2021)

standards_entries.name: Promote the wellbeing and independence of individuals and carers while protecting them from harm
standards_entries.description: Social service workers must report and challenge dangerous, abusive or discriminatory behaviour; follow safety procedures; tell employers about resource or operational matters affecting safe care delivery; report impaired fitness to practise of colleagues; be open when practice causes harm; cooperate with investigations; work with individuals to address concerns and complaints; and use power responsibly.
standards_entries.keywords: ["wellbeing", "independence", "harm prevention", "safeguarding", "reporting", "whistleblowing", "speaking up", "duty of candour", "safety procedures", "complaints", "feedback", "power", "abuse reporting"]
standards_entries.sub_outcomes: [{"ref": "3.1", "desc": "Report allegations of harm, challenge and report any dangerous, abusive or discriminatory behaviour"}, {"ref": "3.2", "desc": "Follow practices, procedures and policies designed to keep workers and other people safe at work"}, {"ref": "3.3", "desc": "Tell employer or relevant authority about any resourcing or operational matter that might affect care or support"}, {"ref": "3.4", "desc": "Tell employer or relevant authority when a colleague's fitness to practise may be impaired"}, {"ref": "3.5", "desc": "Be open and honest with employer, individuals and carers when practice has or may have caused harm or loss"}, {"ref": "3.6", "desc": "Cooperate with any investigations by employer, SSSC or relevant authority into fitness to practise"}, {"ref": "3.7", "desc": "Work with individuals and carers to give and receive feedback, raise concerns and complaints, and act upon them"}, {"ref": "3.8", "desc": "Recognise and use responsibly the power and authority held when working with individuals, carers and colleagues"}]
standards_entries.source: Scottish Social Services Council — Code of Practice for Social Service Workers (2024)

standards_entries.name: Recognise that individuals have the right to take risks and work with them to understand and manage those risks
standards_entries.description: Social service workers must support informed choices about potential and actual risks; follow risk assessment policies; take steps to reduce identified risks; and ensure relevant colleagues and agencies are informed about risk assessment findings.
standards_entries.keywords: ["risk", "positive risk taking", "informed choice", "risk assessment", "risk management", "autonomy", "safety", "harm reduction"]
standards_entries.sub_outcomes: [{"ref": "4.1", "desc": "Work with individuals to make informed choices about potential and actual risks to themselves or others"}, {"ref": "4.2", "desc": "Follow risk assessment policies and procedures to assess whether behaviour presents a risk of harm"}, {"ref": "4.3", "desc": "Take necessary steps to reduce the risks of individuals harming themselves or others"}, {"ref": "4.4", "desc": "Make sure that individuals, relevant colleagues and agencies are informed about the findings and implications of risk assessments"}]
standards_entries.source: Scottish Social Services Council — Code of Practice for Social Service Workers (2024)

standards_entries.name: Be accountable for the quality of work and take responsibility for maintaining and improving knowledge and skills
standards_entries.description: Social service workers must meet relevant standards of practice; maintain accurate records; tell employers about personal circumstances affecting job competence; seek support when uncertain; engage in supervision to reflect on practice and development; maintain CPL (Continuous Professional Learning) to improve knowledge and skills; work openly with colleagues; understand responsibility for delegated work; and work in a trauma-informed way.
standards_entries.keywords: ["accountability", "quality of work", "records management", "documentation", "professional development", "CPL", "continuous professional learning", "supervision", "reflection", "delegated work", "competence", "trauma-informed practice", "partnership working", "fitness to practise"]
standards_entries.sub_outcomes: [{"ref": "5.1", "desc": "Meet relevant standards of practice and work in a lawful, safe and effective way"}, {"ref": "5.2", "desc": "Maintain clear, accurate and up-to-date records in line with policies and procedures"}, {"ref": "5.3", "desc": "Tell employer about personal circumstances or experiences that may affect ability to do job competently and safely"}, {"ref": "5.4", "desc": "Ask for support if not adequately prepared or unsure how to proceed"}, {"ref": "5.5", "desc": "Prepare for and engage in supervision to reflect on development, learning needs, wellbeing and practice"}, {"ref": "5.6", "desc": "Maintain continuous professional learning (CPL) to improve knowledge and skills and contribute to others' development"}, {"ref": "5.7", "desc": "Cooperate and work inclusively and openly with colleagues and treat them with respect"}, {"ref": "5.8", "desc": "Work in a way that is informed by an understanding of the impact that trauma may have on individuals, carers and colleagues"}, {"ref": "5.9", "desc": "Be responsible for the work delegated to others"}, {"ref": "5.10", "desc": "Respect the roles and expertise of colleagues from other professions and work in partnership with them"}, {"ref": "5.11", "desc": "Recognise and respect the roles, expertise and experience of carers, families and relevant others"}, {"ref": "5.12", "desc": "Invite and listen to feedback from individuals, carers and others and use this to improve practice"}]
standards_entries.source: Scottish Social Services Council — Code of Practice for Social Service Workers (2024)

standards_entries.name: Management of records
standards_entries.description: Clear, documented systems are in place for the management of records in accordance with legislative requirements. Records must be accurate, legible, stored securely and retained for required periods. Service users and their representatives must be able to access their own records. Electronic records must be password-protected.
standards_entries.keywords: ["records management", "record keeping", "accuracy", "legibility", "secure storage", "data retention", "data protection", "GDPR", "access to records", "electronic records", "password protection", "confidentiality"]
standards_entries.source: RQIA — Domiciliary Care Agencies Minimum Standards (DHSSPS, August 2021)

standards_entries.name: Uphold public trust and confidence
standards_entries.description: Social service workers must not abuse, harm, neglect or exploit individuals, carers or colleagues; must not abuse trust or misuse personal information; must not form unprofessional relationships; must not discriminate or condone discrimination; must not put people at unnecessary risk; and must not behave in a way that brings into question suitability to work in social services — in or outside work.
standards_entries.keywords: ["public trust", "professional conduct", "integrity", "exploitation", "abuse of trust", "confidentiality", "professional relationships", "discrimination", "fitness to practise", "SSSC registration", "conduct outside work", "social media"]
standards_entries.sub_outcomes: [{"ref": "6.1", "desc": "Must not abuse, harm, neglect or exploit individuals, carers or colleagues"}, {"ref": "6.2", "desc": "Must not abuse the trust of individuals, carers or colleagues, or misuse information about them"}, {"ref": "6.3", "desc": "Must not form unprofessional or harmful relationships with individuals or carers"}, {"ref": "6.4", "desc": "Must not discriminate against individuals, carers or colleagues"}, {"ref": "6.5", "desc": "Must not condone any discrimination by individuals, carers or colleagues"}, {"ref": "6.6", "desc": "Must not put self or other people at unnecessary risk"}, {"ref": "6.7", "desc": "Must not behave, while in or outside work, in a way that would bring suitability to work in social services into question"}]
standards_entries.source: Scottish Social Services Council — Code of Practice for Social Service Workers (2024)

standards_entries.name: Service users' involvement
standards_entries.description: The views of service users and their carers/representatives shape the quality of services provided by the agency. Agencies must actively seek feedback, involve service users in assessments and reviews, and act on their views to improve care delivery.
standards_entries.keywords: ["service user involvement", "feedback", "views", "carers", "representatives", "participation", "person-centred", "involvement in reviews", "satisfaction survey", "individual needs", "quality improvement"]
standards_entries.source: RQIA — Domiciliary Care Agencies Minimum Standards (DHSSPS, August 2021)

standards_entries.name: Referral arrangements
standards_entries.description: Referral arrangements ensure the service user's identified needs can be met by the agency. The agency must carry out an assessment of needs before agreeing to provide care, and must not accept a referral if needs cannot be safely met.
standards_entries.keywords: ["referral", "needs assessment", "suitability", "care needs", "risk assessment", "pre-admission assessment", "eligibility", "care and support needs", "commissioning"]
standards_entries.source: RQIA — Domiciliary Care Agencies Minimum Standards (DHSSPS, August 2021)

standards_entries.name: Management of medicines
standards_entries.description: The agency has arrangements to ensure that care workers manage medicines safely and securely. This includes written policies, trained staff, secure storage, accurate recording (MAR charts), and clear protocols for self-administration, assistance, and safe disposal. Medicine errors must be reported and investigated.
standards_entries.keywords: ["medicines management", "medication", "MAR chart", "controlled drugs", "safe storage", "administration", "medicine errors", "self-administration", "trained staff", "medication policy", "disposal", "prescriptions"]
standards_entries.source: RQIA — Domiciliary Care Agencies Minimum Standards (DHSSPS, August 2021)

standards_entries.name: Management and control of operations
standards_entries.description: Management systems and arrangements are in place that support and promote the delivery of quality care services. The registered person and manager must ensure the agency is conducted with sufficient care, competence and skill. Clear governance, oversight systems, and quality assurance must be demonstrable.
standards_entries.keywords: ["management systems", "governance", "quality assurance", "oversight", "competence", "registered person", "registered manager", "operational control", "quality review", "service improvement", "audit", "accountability"]
standards_entries.source: RQIA — Domiciliary Care Agencies Minimum Standards (DHSSPS, August 2021)

standards_entries.name: Recruitment of staff
standards_entries.description: Staff are recruited and employed in accordance with relevant statutory employment legislation. This includes AccessNI criminal record checks, satisfactory references, verification of qualifications, NISCC registration checks, and health assessments. Agencies must not employ persons who are unsuitable to work with vulnerable adults.
standards_entries.keywords: ["recruitment", "AccessNI", "criminal record check", "DBS", "references", "qualifications", "NISCC registration", "employment checks", "fitness to work", "vetting", "safer recruitment", "employment legislation"]
standards_entries.source: RQIA — Domiciliary Care Agencies Minimum Standards (DHSSPS, August 2021)

standards_entries.name: Staff training and development
standards_entries.description: Staff are trained for their roles and responsibilities. All care workers must complete the NISCC Induction Programme within agreed timescales. Mandatory training must include safeguarding, manual handling, medicines management, infection control and fire safety. A training needs analysis must be conducted and training records maintained.
standards_entries.keywords: ["training", "NISCC induction", "induction programme", "mandatory training", "safeguarding training", "manual handling", "medicines training", "infection control", "training records", "training needs analysis", "CPD", "professional development", "skills development", "competency"]
standards_entries.source: RQIA — Domiciliary Care Agencies Minimum Standards (DHSSPS, August 2021)

standards_entries.name: Staff supervision and appraisal
standards_entries.description: Staff are supervised and their performance appraised to promote the delivery of quality care and services. Supervision must be regular, documented and support staff development. Annual appraisals must identify training needs and personal development goals. Supervision records must be maintained securely.
standards_entries.keywords: ["supervision", "appraisal", "performance management", "staff development", "regular supervision", "documented supervision", "supervision records", "annual appraisal", "training needs", "personal development", "reflective practice", "line management"]
standards_entries.source: RQIA — Domiciliary Care Agencies Minimum Standards (DHSSPS, August 2021)

standards_entries.name: Protection of vulnerable adults and safeguarding children
standards_entries.description: Service users are protected from abuse. Agencies must have a safeguarding policy, a designated safeguarding lead, and ensure all staff receive safeguarding training. All allegations and concerns must be reported immediately to the designated person and the appropriate Trust. Agencies must follow Northern Ireland adult safeguarding procedures and work collaboratively with statutory agencies.
standards_entries.keywords: ["safeguarding", "abuse", "neglect", "vulnerable adults", "safeguarding lead", "safeguarding policy", "reporting concerns", "allegations", "HSC Trust", "adult safeguarding procedures", "NIAPSA", "safeguarding training", "whistleblowing", "financial abuse", "exploitation", "restraint"]
standards_entries.source: RQIA — Domiciliary Care Agencies Minimum Standards (DHSSPS, August 2021)

standards_entries.name: Complaints
standards_entries.description: All complaints are taken seriously and dealt with promptly and effectively. The agency must have a clear complaints procedure accessible to service users and carers. Complaints must be investigated, and the complainant informed of the outcome and any action taken within 28 days. Complaints must be analysed to identify service improvements.
standards_entries.keywords: ["complaints", "complaints procedure", "investigation", "resolution", "28-day response", "complainant rights", "complaints analysis", "service improvement", "RQIA complaints", "advocate", "NIPSO"]
standards_entries.source: RQIA — Domiciliary Care Agencies Minimum Standards (DHSSPS, August 2021)

standards_entries.name: Safe and healthy working practices
standards_entries.description: The agency has systems that ensure safe and healthy working practices for staff and service users. This includes risk assessments for care workers visiting service users' homes, lone working policies, manual handling procedures, infection prevention and control, and appropriate PPE provision. Staff wellbeing must be actively promoted.
standards_entries.keywords: ["health and safety", "risk assessment", "lone working", "manual handling", "infection prevention", "infection control", "PPE", "personal protective equipment", "staff wellbeing", "COSHH", "home environment risk", "first aid"]
standards_entries.source: RQIA — Domiciliary Care Agencies Minimum Standards (DHSSPS, August 2021)

standards_entries.name: Statement of purpose
standards_entries.description: The registered person must compile a written statement of purpose detailing the home's aims and objectives, the facilities and services provided, the philosophy of care, resident numbers and needs, admission criteria, and complaints procedure. A copy must be supplied to RQIA and made available to residents and their representatives.
standards_entries.keywords: ["statement of purpose", "aims and objectives", "philosophy of care", "RQIA", "facilities", "services", "admission criteria", "care home information"]
standards_entries.source: RQIA — The Residential Care Homes Regulations (Northern Ireland) 2005

standards_entries.name: Requirements to ensure quality of care and other service provision
standards_entries.description: Care and services must meet individual needs, reflect best practice and use appropriate aids and equipment. Food and drink must be adequate, nutritious, varied and suitable for residents' specific dietary, cultural, and clinical needs. Equipment must be suitable, maintained, and used correctly.
standards_entries.keywords: ["quality of care", "individual needs", "best practice", "food and drink", "nutrition", "hydration", "equipment", "aids", "dietary needs", "cultural needs", "special diets"]
standards_entries.source: RQIA — The Residential Care Homes Regulations (Northern Ireland) 2005

standards_entries.name: Health and welfare of residents
standards_entries.description: The home must promote residents' health and welfare, enabling them to make decisions about their own care. Residents' wishes and feelings must be ascertained and taken into account. Medicine management must be safe and well-documented. The home must respect residents' privacy, dignity, and diversity, and staff must maintain professional relationships.
standards_entries.keywords: ["health and welfare", "informed decisions", "wishes and feelings", "dignity", "privacy", "medicines management", "medication records", "infection prevention", "diversity", "respect", "professional relationships", "person-centred care"]
standards_entries.source: RQIA — The Residential Care Homes Regulations (Northern Ireland) 2005

standards_entries.name: Further requirements as to health and welfare
standards_entries.description: Residents must have arrangements to register with a GP and receive necessary professional services. The home must be free from hazards, with safe systems for moving and handling. Measures to prevent harm and abuse are mandatory. Restraint may only be used in exceptional circumstances and must be recorded. Training in first aid is required.
standards_entries.keywords: ["GP registration", "professional services", "hazard-free environment", "risk management", "moving and handling", "manual handling", "safeguarding", "abuse prevention", "restraint", "first aid training", "falls prevention"]
standards_entries.source: RQIA — The Residential Care Homes Regulations (Northern Ireland) 2005

standards_entries.name: Assessment of residents
standards_entries.description: Before admitting a resident, their needs must be assessed by a qualified person. The registered person must confirm in writing that the home is suitable for the resident's needs. Assessments must consider physical, mental, cultural and social needs. Assessments must be reviewed at least annually or when needs change.
standards_entries.keywords: ["needs assessment", "pre-admission assessment", "suitability", "holistic assessment", "physical needs", "mental needs", "cultural needs", "social needs", "annual review", "assessment review", "qualified assessor"]
standards_entries.source: RQIA — The Residential Care Homes Regulations (Northern Ireland) 2005

standards_entries.name: Residents' care plan
standards_entries.description: A written care plan must be prepared in consultation with the resident or their representative, outlining how their needs will be met. The care plan must be available to the resident, kept under regular review, and revised to reflect changing needs. Residents must be notified of any revisions.
standards_entries.keywords: ["care plan", "person-centred care plan", "care planning", "consultation", "resident involvement", "care plan review", "changing needs", "individual outcomes", "representative", "care plan update"]
standards_entries.source: RQIA — The Residential Care Homes Regulations (Northern Ireland) 2005

standards_entries.name: Review of quality of care and other service provision
standards_entries.description: Systems must be maintained for reviewing the quality of care and services at least annually. A report of the review must be supplied to RQIA and made available to residents. The review must include consultation with residents and their representatives and analyse incidents, complaints, and areas for improvement.
standards_entries.keywords: ["quality review", "annual review", "quality assurance", "RQIA report", "resident feedback", "incident analysis", "complaints analysis", "quality improvement", "governance"]
standards_entries.source: RQIA — The Residential Care Homes Regulations (Northern Ireland) 2005

standards_entries.name: Records
standards_entries.description: Comprehensive records must be maintained for each resident and for the home overall, as specified in Schedules 3 and 4 of the Regulations. Records must be up-to-date, available to authorised persons, and retained for at least 6 years. Service users must be informed about how to access their personal records.
standards_entries.keywords: ["record keeping", "resident records", "care records", "incident records", "staff records", "duty rosters", "training records", "complaint records", "6-year retention", "data protection", "GDPR", "access to records"]
standards_entries.source: RQIA — The Residential Care Homes Regulations (Northern Ireland) 2005

standards_entries.name: Staffing
standards_entries.description: The home must have suitably qualified, competent and experienced staff in appropriate numbers at all times. Staff must receive appraisal and training, be supported to maintain professional registration (NISCC), and enabled to gain further qualifications. Adequate supervision must be provided and job descriptions given to all staff.
standards_entries.keywords: ["staffing levels", "qualified staff", "competent staff", "staff appraisal", "training", "NISCC registration", "professional registration", "qualifications", "supervision", "job description", "staffing policy", "care workers"]
standards_entries.source: RQIA — The Residential Care Homes Regulations (Northern Ireland) 2005

standards_entries.name: Fitness of workers
standards_entries.description: Persons employed must be fit to work in the home, with satisfactory background information including AccessNI criminal record checks, authentic references, and verification of qualifications and experience. This applies both to directly employed staff and those employed by third parties working at the home.
standards_entries.keywords: ["fitness to work", "AccessNI", "criminal record check", "references", "qualifications", "employment vetting", "safer recruitment", "integrity", "character check", "third party staff", "agency staff"]
standards_entries.source: RQIA — The Residential Care Homes Regulations (Northern Ireland) 2005

standards_entries.name: Staff views as to conduct of the home
standards_entries.description: Arrangements must be made to enable staff to inform the registered person, RQIA, and local HSC Trust, in confidence, of their views on matters affecting the care, safety or welfare of residents. This underpins a culture of openness, transparency and psychological safety.

standards_entries.description: Relevant Codes of Practice — including the NISCC Code of Practice for Social Care Workers — must be made available to staff. standards_entries.description: The registered person must notify RQIA without delay of resident deaths (including circumstances), outbreaks of serious infectious disease, serious injuries, events adversely affecting care, theft, burglary, accidents, or allegations of misconduct. standards_entries.description: Social care workers must treat each person as an individual, treat them with respect and compassion, empower service users and carers to communicate their views, support their right to control their lives and make informed choices, gain appropriate consent, and respect and maintain the dignity and privacy of service users.

standards_entries.description: Workers must not abuse, neglect or harm service users, carers or colleagues; not exploit service users or abuse trust; not form inappropriate personal relationships; not discriminate unlawfully; not put themselves or others at unnecessary risk; not behave in a way that questions their suitability; and use social media appropriately.

supervision_uploads.full_text:
Supervision with Harvey
 Generated 01 Aug 2026 18:06 UTC
Test Manager
Date: 2026-07-30 · Manager: Admin
MINTY
Do I have to talk?
ALEX
Yeah.
MINTY
Can I be facetious?
ALEX
Absolutely, whatever you want.
MINTY
So, walk me through how you organised cover for your upcoming holiday plans that we discussed in our last
supervision meeting.
ALEX
I told you, well, I requested the annual levy that was approved. We then discussed who best to speak to in
terms of covering for me. You looked at the rotors and then you suggested that you would speak to Elaine.
MINTY
Right. OK, cool. And tell me how you've been looking after your own well-being following the intensive
personal care and post-lunch support noted in the 18th of July practice observation with MC.
ALEX
I just go home and cry.
MINTY
Yeah, that's understandable. M is a baggage.
ALEX
M needs to be shot.
MINTY
So, tell me about a situation where you were working with MC in a meaningful activity during your day out on
July the 24th and how you anticipated her needs based on preferences recorded in the feedback.
ALEX
Well, as we know, M loves art. So, I suggested that we go to a local pottery painting place. And when we
arrived, I obviously explained that M was in a wheelchair and they made accommodations to fit her
wheelchair at a table. They brought over different things that were able to be painted and she made her
choice. She chose the colours and we had a lovely cup of tea while we were doing it.
MINTY
Awesome. I suspect that's probably why she gave you such positive feedback. So, can you give me a
specific example of how you prepared for the lunchtime session in terms of checking dietary records and so
on for the 18th of July observation and whatnot?
ALEX
For M?
MINTY
No, this wasn't specifically M. This was the sort of the lunchtime session that we did.
ALEX
Well, we have a whiteboard in the kitchen, which has every resident's allergies, preferences, the way they
have to have their food. So, like D, for example, all of her food has to be pureed. And then we have a binder
which has all of the instructions on, you know, what temperature the food must be got to, et cetera, et cetera.
MINTY
OK, cool. I checked that according to who was in the lunch that day.
MINTY
Sure. Awesome. That sounds really, really good. So, you know, when you filled out an incident report form
for the frayed lamp cable in M's room. And can you just describe to me the steps you took to clarify the
escalation pathway when Tony wasn't available? Tony's the maintenance man, by the way.
ALEX
Well, I spoke to my supervisor and asked who best to speak to because Tony wasn't there.
MINTY
What did they say?

ALEX
They said speak to Tom.
MINTY
Awesome. And did you kind of follow it through? Did Tom resolve the issue?
ALEX
Yeah.
MINTY
Awesome. So can you give me a specific example of how the shadowing shift that you did on that specific bit
of equipment that Tom uses that we talked about in the last supervision, how that impacted on your
confidence in supporting the residents that use that bit of equipment?
ALEX
What, when I shadowed you?
MINTY
Yeah. What are you asking me?
ALEX
So an example of how that shadow shift impacted your confidence afterwards in supporting the residents.
MINTY
Well, yeah. Well, I'm very much a visual learner. Like I need to see I can't I don't like to just read instructions
or to be told I need to see what's happening. So me being able to observe it being used, you know, made me
feel confident to use it by myself the next time.
ALEX
Cool. So so that that that sort of style of learning is something we need to think about in the future as well, is
it?
MINTY
Yeah, I think everyone has a different style of learning. I mean, you know, two people might have the same
style, but it's not really the third person. So things like just reading instructions, it just doesn't compute in my
head. It just I just don't retain the information, whereas when I actually watch someone do something or even
practice with someone instructing me there, then it's then I feel confident.
ALEX
OK, cool. Well, we'll endeavor to kind of make a note of that for future sessions and whatnot. So when you
went into town with M on the 24th of July and this comes under the achievement section, I said earlier about
the great feedback that she gave you. What do you think it was that you did that day that reflects your person
centred approach, but meant that she gave you such great feedback?
MINTY
I think I think in the past she's been with people who have just thought, oh, we'll just look around the shops
and go to Foster. And because that's what old people do in town. But we often talk about art and the fact that
she used to like to paint. And I think she was surprised at the suggestion because it made her feel like she
was listened to. And her preferences were considered in that activity in town. And she did say, like, I do like
going around shops, but where it gets a bit repetitive and she felt like she could be creative again. And the
fact that, you know, we whilst I chose the place, I chose it because I knew it was accessible and local. She
obviously got the choice of what to paint. She got the choice of what colours to use and what design to do,
whilst also having her needs understood and met in terms of accessibility and that kind of thing.
ALEX
And did the when when you were at the place, did they have to make any sort of special arrangement? You
know, did they have to do anything particularly special to accommodate her?
MINTY
Luckily, there weren't any steps or anything, but they did kind of shift the chairs and stuff around so that she
had enough space to sit at the table. And, you know, in her wheelchair, remain comfortable in her
wheelchair. She didn't have to, you know what she's like, she doesn't like transferring out her wheelchair.
ALEX
Yeah, quite. I mean, the fact that she said in her feedback that she felt like herself again, it's just you should
be really proud. It's so good. It's so good. It's exactly what what we're working towards at Oakwood
Residential. So I just want to go back to the frayed lamp cable and the uncertainty that you experienced in
the moment because Tony wasn't there. If that happened again, do you feel confident that, you know, this
time you went to your supervisor? They said speak to Tom. Do you feel confident that if there was some
other situation where somebody wasn't available that you'd have a path or a route?

MINTY
I do, but there wasn't any kind of there wasn't any communication to, you know, something like a
maintenance person. Tony is, you know, he's there every day, you know, nine to five, pretty much. And he
was just on a course that day.
ALEX
Yeah, but there's not.
MINTY
There's not. I think when it when it's just random staff, you know, like carers like me who are going off on a
course or who are going on holiday, whether it doesn't really impact us because we the people who are there
doing the caring are doing our caring. Like we don't really need to know that someone else isn't here.
Obviously, if our supervisor is not going to be here, we get told that anyway. But when it's someone who like
anyone could rely on at any moment in the day, I think it would be good if there was maybe a communication
that went out via email or text to say, like, by the way, just let you know, like Tony, like Tony, the
maintenance guy or like Leslie, the receptionist or like people that everyone could go to at any point in the
day for a reason, is told like they're not going to be in this week because they're on holiday or whatever. So
this is the protocol to get stuff fixed or to have stuff printed out or whatever. Because I felt a bit like, well,
what if my supervisor wasn't in that day? Like who would I ask to then find out who to contact about this like
potentially dangerous situation?
ALEX
So we perhaps need to there's a maybe a wider learning issue there. We need to have a bit of a team
meeting about because obviously it doesn't happen that often. Tony's not on a course that often. But you're
right.
MINTY
And it's not I'm not saying that we need to know everyone in the businesses movement. But it's just those
people that are like everyone can rely on.
ALEX
I get it. Yeah.
MINTY
Yeah. Or like.
MINTY
Yeah. Or or like the office manager.
ALEX
Sure.
MINTY
That kind of thing, because I know like Kelly, my supervisors like brush off her feet and for me to be like, you
know, it takes away from my time doing my job, having to go and find her or call her to find out what to do
about this. Because, you know, because I've suddenly found out that Tony's not here.
ALEX
Sure.
MINTY
And it needs sorting like now.
ALEX
Yeah.
MINTY
Yeah. Quite.
ALEX
OK. I mean, it's all good stuff. And this is why supervision is so important. So just a kind of a final question to
sort of draw things to a close. So when M said that she didn't want to make a fuss, when you spotted the
frayed cable and she was like, oh, you know, I knew about it. I didn't want to make a fuss. Can you think of
what having dealt with that situation? If you're in a situation with another resident, how we can empower
residents? Actually, it's OK to say something.
MINTY
Well, I said to her at the time, I was like, M, your safety is not a fuss. Like that's why we're here. You know,
so it's nothing for you to worry about. It's our job to make sure that not that just that you can like, you know.
Use the bath safely or have your toes done for you. It's like we've got to make sure that your environment is
safe as well. And your health and safety is like the most important thing to us. So it's never a fuss.
ALEX
Yeah, that's as I like that. Actually, your safety is not a fuss because I bet there's lots of people that think.

MINTY
Yeah. And, you know, like we're I mean, to put it bluntly, we're paid to do it. Like that's our part of our job.
And, you know, most people I think here want to do a good job. You know, we have not only do we care
about our residents, but we also have, you know, pride in the work that we do.
ALEX
Yeah.
MINTY
So to say, you know, I just said to you, it's not a fuss.
ALEX
Yeah. And hopefully that's a reflection of our company values and all of that.
MINTY
When I said that to her, she she kind of said, oh, yeah, no, you're right. Like, you know, I said to her, what
would be a fuss would be if you touched it and electrocuted it, that would be a fuss.
ALEX
Yeah.
MINTY
Yeah. Imagine the paperwork if you did get electrocuted.
ALEX
So she laughed at that.
MINTY
Oh, well, that's good.
ALEX
Is there anything else that you want to cover that we haven't covered?
MINTY
No, I don't think so.
ALEX
OK, fabulous. All right. Thank you.

supervision_uploads.full_text:
Supervision Transcript
Setting: Oakwood Residential Care Home Manager: Sarah Thompson, Team Leader Supervisee: Jane Smith, Care Worker Date: 14 August 2025 
Sarah: Right Jane, thanks for coming in. How are you doing today?
Jane: Yeah I'm okay. Fine.
Sarah: You sure? You seem a little quiet.
Jane: Sorry. Yeah I'm fine. Just tired I think.
Sarah: Okay. Well let's make a start. I've had a look back at last month's supervision and we said you were going to finish your moving and handling refresher by the end of July. Did you get that done?
Jane: No. Sorry. I meant to but it just didn't happen.
Sarah: Okay, no worries, we'll come back to that. How have you been finding the work generally?
Jane: It's been... yeah. It's been fine. Some days are harder than others.
Sarah: What's making it hard?
Jane: [pause] Sorry. [pause] I don't know. I just... [voice breaks] Sorry, I don't know why I'm crying. This is embarrassing.
Sarah: Hey, don't apologise. Take your time. There's no rush here.
Jane: [pause] It's just been a lot lately. At home as well as here. I'm just really tired.
Sarah: When you say at home as well, do you want to tell me a bit more about that? Only if you want to.
Jane: It's just... things have been difficult. With my mum. She's not well and I'm trying to look after her and work full time and I just feel like I'm not doing anything very well at the moment.
Sarah: That sounds really hard Jane. Caring for someone at home on top of a full time job in care is a lot for anyone. How long has this been going on?
Jane: A few months. Since about April.
Sarah: And have you spoken to anyone about it? Your GP, or anyone?
Jane: No. I just keep thinking it'll get better.
Sarah: Okay. I'm really glad you told me. I want you to know that's exactly what this time is for. Can I ask, has anything happened at work that's been particularly difficult, or is it mainly the situation at home that's affecting you?
Jane: Mainly home I think. But sometimes when I'm here and something difficult happens with a resident it just... it hits differently at the moment. Last week when Mrs Collins was really poorly I found that quite hard. I kept thinking about my mum.
Sarah: That makes a lot of sense. You're carrying a lot. Have you heard of our Employee Assistance Programme?
Jane: No.
Sarah: Okay, so we have a confidential support line you can ring any time, it's completely separate from work, they offer counselling and practical advice. I'm going to get you the details today before you leave. And I also want to think with you about whether there's anything we can do to make things a little easier at work while things are tough at home. Is there anything that would help?
Jane: I don't want any special treatment.
Sarah: It's not special treatment, it's just good management. Even small things — if there are shifts or particular tasks that are harder for you at the moment, I'd rather know.
Jane: Maybe just... I don't know. Sometimes the night shifts are really hard because I'm already tired. But I don't want to let anyone down.
Sarah: You're not letting anyone down. Let me have a look at the rota and see what I can do. No promises but I'll try. How are you feeling now, compared to when you came in?
Jane: A bit better actually. Sorry for getting upset.
Sarah: Please don't apologise. This is what supervision is for. I'm going to make a note of what we've talked about today and I'll get you those EAP details. The moving and handling — let's set a new date, how does end of September sound?
Jane: Yeah that's fine.
Sarah: Okay. And I want to check in with you again in a couple of weeks, just informally, not a full supervision. Is that okay?
Jane: Yeah. Thank you Sarah.
